episodes.209935: A front lifted into the area on the 3rd of March and then continued to ripple through the region over the next couple of days. Rain initially spread southwest to northeast across the area on the afternoon of the 3rd, then the focus of moderate to heavy rain became more confined to southeast Ohio and north central West Virginia during the evening and overnight hours. Another wave of showers pushed across the area after daybreak, however precipitation amounts were fairly light. A lull in precipitation occurred mid to late morning, then precipitation began streaming back into the area from the west during the afternoon.||In the first twenty-four hours of the event, precipitation amounts ranged from around half an inch to two inches across northern West Virginia. Meanwhile, amounts generally remained under an inch within the southern half of the state. Highest amounts were observed in a narrow swath across Wood, Jackson, Wirt, Ritchie, Calhoun, and Gilmer counties. Another one to two and a half inches of rain fell across portions of the state as additional rounds of rain, and some thunderstorms, traversed the area into the morning of the 6th. Rises on local creeks, streams, and smaller rivers primarily led to flooded roads in Wood, Gilmer, and Ritchie Counties on the 4th, then runoff prompted minor flooding to develop on the Tygart Valley River at Mill Creek the morning of the 6th. Flooding came to an end once precipitation tapered off during the day.
episodes.209940: Low level moisture streamed into the region on the morning of the fifth leading to low stratus for much of the day. Sufficient clearing occurred in the afternoon to destabilize the atmosphere near a warm front and dryline. Thunderstorms initially developed along these surface features over the Rolling Plains. Thunderstorms quickly became severe over Hall County where a swath of severe hail was observed between Lakeview and Memphis along Texas State Highway 256. Reports of hail ranged in size from penny size to 2.25 inches in diameter.
episodes.209947: A combination of 0.50-0.75 of rain and snowmelt led to minor flooding across Route 249 (Long Run Road) in Westfield Township, Tioga County during the evening of March 5, 2026.
episodes.210078: During March 3 to March 7, 2026, large surface high pressure from the southeastern United States into the Atlantic focused a broad fetch of Gulf moisture northward into the Midwest.  A quasi-stationary frontal boundary near the Ohio Valley provided lift and focused, at times heavy rainfall over much of central Indiana, especially along the valley of the East Fork White River, and its tributaries northeast of Columbus through east-central central Indiana.||From the morning of the 3rd through dawn on the 4th, heavy rainfall over the watershed of the East Fork White's headwaters totaled mainly 2.00-3.75 inches.  Additional 1-day rainfall to dawn on the 5th, along the river's main stem from Columbus down through Martin County totaled generally 1.50-3.00 inches.  Further 2.5-day rainfall through late on the 7th was generally 1.00-2.00 inches along this main stem.  Overall 4.5-day rainfall totals were 4.00 to 6.00 inches for most portions of the entire East Fork White watershed.||Resultant widespread significant river flooding, including adjacent lowlands, from the Columbus area downstream through Jackson County, Lawrence County, and Martin County necessitated multiple water rescues.   Four persons over three counties perished when swept away by flood waters from the 6th to the 9th - three in motor vehicles and one in an airboat that encountered mechanical failure.
episodes.210095: An incoming trough and plentiful moisture allowed for a couple of showers and thunderstorms to develop in the central and eastern Permian Basin of west Texas. One storm near Penwell was able to briefly produce quarter-sized hail.
episodes.210302: On the afternoon of March 6th, 2026, a lone supercell developed in La Porte County, IN and tracked northeast into Lower Michigan. The supercell moved through Cass, St Joseph, Branch, and Calhoun counties. NWS storm damage surveys from NWS Northern Indiana and NWS Grand Rapids found that the parent supercell spawned 4 tornadoes across Lower Michigan, ranging from EF-0 to EF-3 intensity. There were numerous reports called in to our office and videos posted on social media by storm chasers, broadcast media, trained spotters, and the public confirming tornado damage in Edwardsburg, Three Rivers, and Union City. The north side of Union Lake in Union City was one of the hardest hit areas with numerous homes taking on significant damage and trees sheared off. Several businesses in the city of Three Rivers also sustained notable damage. Unfortunately, there were multiple fatalities and injuries across Lower Michigan.
episodes.210303: A supercell thunderstorm moved through La Porte County on the afternoon of March 6 and produced 1.75 inch diameter hail. The storm went on to produce multiple tornadoes in southern Michigan.
episodes.210337: Scattered thunderstorms moved across northeast Illiniois during the afternoon of March 6th producing heavy rain, localized flooding and localized severe winds.
episodes.210339: Scattered thunderstorms moved across southern Lake Michigan during the afternoon and early evening of March 6th producing localized severe winds.
episodes.210474: During the late evening of Thursday March 5th, a supercell thunderstorm tracked out of northern Oklahoma and into southern Kansas. As the storm crossed into Kansas, the rotation strengthened and eventually produced a couple of tornadoes over western Sumner County. One tornado damaged a few farm outbuildings, multiple trees and overturned a pumpjack. It was rated an EF-2. The other tornado damaged farm outbuildings and utility poles. Thankfully there were no injuries or fatalities. The storm produced damaging straightline winds as well. ||Additional storms developed across central Kansas with up to nickel to quarter sized hail reported. There were storms with winds around 60 mph as well including one that damaged a cedar tree.
episodes.210603: Scattered severe thunderstorms impacted portions of western and northern Oklahoma from the late evening of the 5th into early morning hours of the 6th. This activity developed in the vicinity of a dryline as a deep upper trough began to establish across the Four Coners. As a nocturnal low-level jet strengthened after sunset, a pair of cyclic tornadic thunderstorms emerged from the eastern Texas Panhandle into northern Oklahoma. In addition to several tornadoes, including a deadly tornado west of Fairview in Major County, large hail and eventually damaging wind gusts were observed with severe convection across the region.
episodes.210604: A deep upper trough, centered across the Four Corners, fostered multiple waves of strong-to-severe convection across the WFO Norman Forecast Area during the morning and early evening of the 6th, and again in the early morning of the 7th. Strong mid-tropospheric flow/wind shear and instability yielded a mix of semi-organized convection, including several supercells, during each storm period. Large hail, damaging wind gusts and a tornado (which occurred during the early evening) were reported.
episodes.210756: Scattered storms developed across northeast Kansas on the evening of March 5. These storms produced mostly small hail, pea to dime sized, with one instance of quarter size hail in Nemaha County.
episodes.211006: Severe thunderstorms developed into eastern Oklahoma during the late afternoon of the 6th, ahead of a surface dry line, and moved across the area through the evening hours. The atmosphere had become strongly unstable across eastern Oklahoma during the afternoon east of the dry line. This instability, combined with very strong low-level and deep-layer wind shear across the region, resulted in the evolution of several long-lived supercell thunderstorms. These supercells produced eleven tornadoes, a couple of which were strong and damaging, large hail up to quarter size, damaging wind gusts, and localized flash flooding.
episodes.211195: An upper-level disturbance interacting with an unseasonably warm and humid airmass triggered a line of thunderstorms in the Illinois River Valley during the late afternoon of March 6th.  As the line progressed eastward, a few of the stronger cells produced marginally severe hail and a few reports of minor wind damage.  A second line of convection formed near the Mississippi River later in the evening and produced a couple wind and hail reports in Fulton County toward midnight.
episodes.211620: As an upper-level trough moved eastward past the Rockies, a favorable environment was in place for severe weather. However, the majority of the moisture, instability and surface convergence occurred south and east of the CWA. Some storms were able to initiate in Barber county and generate severe hail before exiting the forecast area.
episodes.212115: Scattered thunderstorms ahead a cold front produced isolated severe weather.
episodes.212116: Scattered thunderstorms ahead a cold front produced isolated severe weather.
episodes.212117: Scattered thunderstorms ahead a cold front produced isolated severe weather.
episodes.212166: Isolated thunderstorms developed across western North Carolina during the afternoon. One storm produced nickel size hail in the foothills.
episodes.212181: On the evening of March 6, 2026, severe thunderstorms brought large hail to eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. As an upper-level trough advanced into the Four Corners region, it induced southwesterly flow aloft and pushed a surface cold front through the local area. Convective development occurred in two distinct phases. Initially, surface-based supercells initiated along the advancing cold front in southwest Iowa, producing large hail. Later in the evening, a second round of elevated supercells developed behind the frontal boundary, affecting eastern Nebraska and extending back into portions of southwest Iowa. During the initial phase, storms in southwest Iowa produced measured hail up to 1.25 inches in diameter near Elliott. The subsequent elevated supercells produced even larger hail, highlighted by a report of 2.50-inch diameter hail near Laurel, Nebraska, along with numerous additional reports of 1.00 to 2.00-inch hail scattered across the region.
episodes.212243: Severe weather impacted lower Michigan on March 6th. 1 tornado occurred in the Grand Rapids County Warning Area while 3 occurred in the Northern Indiana County Warning Area.
episodes.212343: A strong Atlantic high-pressure system produced fresh to strong easterly winds across Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands. The resulting tight pressure gradient generated choppy to rough seas and a high risk of rip currents across the region.
episodes.212782: Larger-scale mid to upper-level troughing worked its way out of the Rockies and onto the Central and Northern Plains on this Friday afternoon. An accompanying surface cold front pushed southeast across the region during the daytime hours, ending up across far southeastern portions of the local forecast area by mid-late afternoon. Scattered thunderstorms developed along this frontal boundary roughly between 3-4 PM CST, having plenty of deeper layer shear to work with and MLCAPE around 1000-1500 j/kg. A few storms strengthened enough to drop large hail across portions of Thayer and Fillmore counties between 4-7 PM CST. The largest hail reported was around Bruning, which had golf ball to tennis ball size hail.

events.narrative: A member of the public reported quarter-sized hail. The time of occurrence is estimated by radar.

Numerous reports from storm chasers, law enforcement, and the public depicted a swath of severe hail. This swath of hail was observed from southwest of Lakeview into the town of Memphis along Texas Highway 256. Hail ranged in size from pennies to 2.25 inches in diameter. No damage was reported.
An OKC television storm chaser observed and photographed a tornado esimated to be about 6 miles west of Putnam. No damage was reported.
Images were shared on social media.
The report was relayed through Spotter Network.
The location is approximate.

This tornado developed near or just southwest of the intersection of County Roads E0560 Road and N2430 Road in Major County where it damaged trees and power poles and twisted a stop sign. The tornado quickly intensified as it approached US-60 west of Fairview. A car along US-60 was hit by this tornado and rolled approximately 520 yards to the northeast. A woman and her daughter were killed in his car. Wooden transmission line poles and standard wooden power poles were broken along and north of US-60. The tornado continued northeast through rural areas of Major County damaging additional trees before dissipating east or southeast of the intersection of E0500 Road and N2460 Road approximately 7 miles west of Fairview.
The location is approximate. The report was relayed by emergency management.
A social media photo showed 1 inch hail. Additionally, the emergency manager reported 0.75 inch hail at the same time and place.
Fairview (FAI2) Mesonet observation.
Fairview (FAI2) Mesonet observation.

This tornado developed just south of US-412 and west of N2520 Road. Along US-412, one home along suffered roof damage, two outbuildings and power poles were damaged. As it moved northeast, additional trees and power poles were damaged before the tornado crossed the Cimarron River. Another home suffered minor damage near the end of the tornado path near E0400 Road about 2 miles west of State Highway 8.
A social media photo of 1.75 inch hail.
Quarter size hail fell in the town of Corning. Report relayed from emergency management.

This tornado developed about 4 miles west-southwest of Helena, or about a mile southeast of the community of McWillie. This tornado moved generally northeast although there was some variability in motion as it moved north of Helena and then south and east of Jet. Power poles were damaged as the tornado crossed State Highway 45 and areas west of Helena. Significant damage was observed along State Highway 58 north of Helena where a number of power poles were broken along a mile stretch of SH-58, and at least three barns were destroyed (EF2) both along SH-58 and east of SH-58 on E0300 Road. The tornado continued to produce tree and power pole damage as it moved northeast. Power poles were broken east of Jet along N2740 Road and along U.S. Highway 64 on both sides of the Alfalfa-Grant County line.  The tornado then moved into Grant County with the centerline crossing the county line just north of U.S. 64.
The location is approximate, and the event time is estimated based on radar observations. The report was relayed by emergency management.

This tornado moved from Alfalfa County into Grant County west of Nash, along and north of U.S. Highway 64. A row of power poles was broken along U.S. 64 on both sides on the Alfalfa-Grant County line with damage consistent with an EF2 tornado The tornado was turning to the left and moving more north-northeast as it moved into Grant County. The tornado continued to damage trees and power poles between the county line and N2760 Road in areas south of E0220 Road. The tornado dissipated near or soon after crossing E0220 Road.

This tornado developed south of Wakita and a mobile home was unroofed and at least two buildings were destroyed along Harper Road. A number of power poles were damaged along State Highway 11 as the tornado moved northeast. Although the last damage was noted by the survey team along State Highway 11, a storm chaser observed the tornado at least a couple of miles farther northeast and the tornado is estimated to have dissipated about 5 miles southeast of Wakita.
Mostly nickel sized hail with a few quarter sized pieces fell.
A tornado developed west of Renfrow and moved north-northwest. Tree damage was reported in the area, although the specific tornado path is estimated.
A storm chaser observed a tornado south of Cheyenne. No damage was reported and the location is estimated to be in southern Roger Mills County about 5 miles west-northwest of Berlin.
A barn was damaged west of Wakita as a tornado moved northeast from west of Wakita to about 1 mile north of Wakita.
Garage with open door was lifted and pushed to the north. There is debris all in that direction. A few metal bins were dented as well. An unanchored swing was moved to the north northeast.
The location is approximate. The report was relayed by emergency management.
The upper floor and roof of barn were pushed to the north and northeast. Part of the roof fell onto the newly built covered area to the north of structure.
A report of a large eastern red cedar tree was snapped at six feet above the ground. The time is estimated from radar data.

A storm survey found a tornado led to damage occurring to the top of a tank battery, an overturned pumpjack, a few snapped power poles and cedar trees. There were additional to damage to multiple outbuildings.

An occluded tornado produced damage to a couple of outbuildings, and it moved several round hay bales. They were strewn on either side of the road. A couple small headstones in the cemetery were knocked over.
The location is approximate, and the event time is estimated based on radar observations.
A tractor-trailer was blown over along U.S. Highway 281. The location is approximate, and the event time is estimated based on radar observations.
A personal weather station had a measured gust to 58 mph.
Alva (ALV2) Mesonet observation.

A combination of 0.50-0.75 of rain and snowmelt led to minor flooding across Route 349 (Long Run Road) in Westfield Township, causing it to be closed between Stevenson Street and Applenap Road for a little over an hour the evening of March 5, 2026.

The Tygart Valley River at Mill Creek rose above a bankfull level of 11 feet on the morning of March 6th, then continued to rise to a crest of around 12 feet later the same morning. The river then receded back below bankfull level that afternoon. Flooding of County Route 39 near the bridge heading out of town occurred in the midst of the river being out of its banks.

River flooding in northeastern Jackson County was exasperated locally by heavy rainfall during the overnight of the 4th-5th around 2.00 inches, with the East Fork White River later cresting at Seymour in major flood stage on the 5th evening.  On the 6th morning around 700EST, a man in an airboat near Courtland, while attempting to rescue individuals stranded in a submerged vehicle, died after the boat experienced mechanical issues, capsized, and was swept under a bridge.
The report was relayed through mPING.

events.narrative: Strong winds and rough seas caused a small recreational vessel carrying four occupants to capsize near Caja de Muerto, south of Ponce. One person drowned while three others were rescued and survived the incident. Hazardous marine conditions were present across the local waters due to enhanced easterly winds associated with a strong Atlantic high-pressure system.
Received a report from the public of 1.75 inch diamater hail near Westville, IN.

A disorganized circulation touched down northwest of the|intersection of Runkle St and Conrad Rd, destroying an attached|garage, and destroying the center part of the home (back windows failed and resulted in front of house blowing out). One fatality, a 12 year|old boy, was confirmed at the home as he was located in the attached garage at the time. A female resident was also injured. The tornado continued|northeast, causing damage to mainly trees with some minor roof|damage as it moved across Yankee St, east of Dailey Rd. The|tornado then widen and intensified with the peak damage occurring|along Harris St, between Hess Rd and M-62 where numerous trees|were snapped or uprooted. Some damage to pole barns and homes|(mainly roofs) was noted. The tornado crossed M-62  and continued|northeast, crossing portions of Oil City Rd and Monette St to|Curtis, Day and Chain Lakes before lifting just east of the|intersection of South and Walnut Rd.
Video shows quarter-size hail.
A tree was blown down along County Road 36 in eastern Geneva county.

Another tornado from the same supercell that produced the|Edwardsburg tornado touched down near Roberts Rd and M60 just|southwest of Three Rivers on Friday afternoon. The tornado|quickly intensified and produced EF-2 damage with estimated wind|speeds of 120-130 mph. Here, the tornado hit a Menards, removing|the roof on the southwest and northwest portions of the building,|along with an exterior wall collapse. One section of an nearby|Uhaul facility was also completely destroyed. The tornado|continued through the heart of Three Rivers, producing EF-1 and|isolated pockets of EF-2 damage to residences and businesses|(including the hospital). The tornado crossed the St. Joseph|River, producing extensive damage to a lumber yard before|uprooting many trees in a local cemetery. The tornado produced|another pocket of EF-2 damage to a double-wide mobile home and a|brand new school transportation facility. Multiple school|trailers were tossed either across the street or inside the|transportation facility itself which had its roof removed. As the|tornado became cut off from the main supercell, it began to jog|more eastward. It produced more damage north of Centreville|including a large barn and additional trees snapped.
Photo received of hail up to a quarter in diameter. Photo taken on Marcellus Rd.
Photo on Facebook shows a hailstone that measured 1.75 inches.  This stone reported fell between Mendon and Three Rivers.
Photo on Facebook shows hail estimated to be between 1 to 1.5 inches in diameter.
NWS employee reported dime to nickel size hail near the Burke County line.

The most intense and deadly tornado of the cyclic tornadic|supercell touched down in northwest Branch county, northwest of|Union Lake between Blossom Rd and Mendon Rd. This tornado was|well photographed from multiple angles, and it quickly turned|into a multi-vortex wedge. After destroying a pole barn and|damaging a residence, the tornado deposited a 500 gallon propane|tank in a field. Drone footage also showed ground scouring in the|same field. The tornado continued northeast and caused the most|widespread and intense damage along Prairie Rose Ln. Every|residence along this stretch was either heavily damaged or|completely destroyed. Tragically, three individuals lost their|lives here when their manufactured homes were lofted and tossed.|One of these trailers was well anchored and tossed approximately|100 yards, badly twisting the frame. Numerous vehicles were also|tossed in this area. The maximum peak intensity of 160 mph was|estimated to be at the corner of Tuttle Rd and Prairie Rose Ln.|This 2 story block home was completely destroyed. Construction|quality and older building codes of all homes in this area|contributed to their failure and precluded the survey team from|being able to rate higher than an EF-3. The tornado continued off|to the northeast into Union City producing EF-1 to EF2 damage|along the way before dissipating at the Branch/Calhoun county|line. Special thanks to the various subject matter experts on the|Quick Response Team that helped NWS Northern Indiana determine|this tornado's intensity.
Severe tree damage and some property damage found in this area.
Exit sign on the highway was blown over.

EF-0 tornado with peak winds around 85 mph began |just west of the intersection of P Drive South and 18 1/2 Mile |Road. The damage path ended near N Drive South between 20 Mile |Road and 21 1/2 Mile Road. Several trees were uprooted along the |path, and some unhealthy trunk snaps. There was minor damage to |some structures, including a roof off a chicken coop, and an |exposed farm outbuilding with some walls collapsed and metal roof|material scattered downfield. The end point had an uprooted tree|or two, but also numerous trees that had limbs recently torn off |presumably not associated with the tornado, as the only torn |limbs were those hanging over the road right-of-way.
A large tree branch was blown down.
A semi truck was blown over.
A grain bin, tree, small sheds, playground set, garage door, and soffit were damaged.
The report was relayed through mPING.
A measured wind gust to 58 mph was reported on Rose Street where a tree limb was blown down onto a car.
The location is approximate.

Video showed a vehicle stranded in flood waters beneath an underpass near Emerald Avenue and East Lincoln Highway. Minor flooding was reported on roadways in Chicago Heights. Thorn Creek in Glenwood reached minor flood stage. Rainfall of 3.06 inches was reported in Park Forest.

events.narrative: The tornado developed approximately four miles northwest of Bristow, west of South 401st West Avenue and north of West 221st Street South. Moving northeast, it crossed South 401st West Avenue, where it destroyed a single-wide mobile home and an outbuilding. As the tornado continued northeast across Highway 16, it uprooted trees and snapped large limbs. At the intersection of Highway 48 and West 181st Street South, the tornado impacted an industrial site, collapsing overhead doors and removing roof sections from two metal buildings. The tornado maintained a northeast track, breaking additional large tree limbs along South 337th West Avenue, before dissipating north of Highway 66. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in the tornado was 100 to 110 mph.
Public mPING report of hail measured at 1.00 inch in diameter.
